For every k-scheme T the T-points of (X \times_k L) \times_L (X \times_k L) are pairs of L-algebra maps L \to \Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)... more concretely, on affine opens X = Spec A, X' = Spec A' one computes
  (A \otimes_k L) \otimes_L (A' \otimes_k L) \cong A \otimes_k L \otimes_k A' \cong (A \otimes_k A') \otimes_k L,
using that an L-algebra map (A\otimes_k L)\otimes_L(A'\otimes_k L) \to B (B an L-algebra) is the same as a pair of k-algebra maps A \to B, A' \to B, i.e. the same as a k-algebra map A\otimes_k A' \to B, i.e. the same as an L-algebra map (A\otimes_k A')\otimes_k L \to B. Gluing gives a canonical isomorphism
  \phi: X_L \times_L X_L \xrightarrow{\sim} V \times_k L =: V_L
over V and over S'. Under \phi the map res is exactly the flat pullback f^*: CH_d(V) \to CH_d(V_L) associated with the projection f: V_L \to V. So the lemma asserts: n \cdot \alpha = f_* f^* \alpha = 0 for \alpha \in \ker(f^*).

STEP 2. f is finite locally free of rank n.  Choose a k-basis e_1,\dots,e_n of the field L (possible since L/k is finite of degree n); thus L \cong k^{\oplus n} as k-module. For any affine open U = Spec B \subset V,
  f^{-1}(U) = Spec(B \otimes_k L), \qquad B \otimes_k L = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{n} B\cdot(1\otimes e_i),
so B\otimes_k L is a free B-module of rank n. Hence f is affine, finite (a finite B-algebra) and locally free of rank n; in particular f is flat of relative dimension 0 and proper.

STEP 3. Claim: for every integral closed subscheme W \subset V of dimension d, one has f_* f^*[W] = n\,[W] in Z_d(V).

3a. The fibre product W \times_V V_L equals W \times_k L. Its structure morphism \rho: W\times_k L \to W is obtained from f by base change, hence is finite locally free of rank n. Write R := \Gamma(U,\mathcal O_W) for a non-empty affine open U = Spec R of W; R is a domain with fraction field K = \kappa(W) = \kappa(\eta), \eta being the generic point of W. Then R\otimes_k L \cong R^{\oplus n} as R-module, so R\otimes_k L is flat over R; it is faithfully flat because for every \mathfrak p \in Spec R the fibre ring \kappa(\mathfrak p)\otimes_k L is a non-zero K'-vector space of dimension n \ge 1, hence has a prime ideal. For a faithfully flat ring map, going-down holds, so every minimal prime of R\otimes_k L contracts to the minimal prime (0) of R. Consequently every irreducible component V_1,\dots,V_r of W\times_k L dominates W, and its generic point \xi_j maps to \eta. (Equivalently: the generic points of W\times_k L are exactly the primes of R\otimes_k L minimal over (0), and they all lie over (0).)

3b. Each V_j is closed in W\times_k L, hence finite over W (a closed subscheme of a finite W-scheme is finite); being dominant and finite, V_j \to W is surjective, and for finite dominant morphisms of integral schemes dimensions agree: \dim V_j = \dim W = d. Thus W\times_k L is equidimensional of dimension d and the cycle [W\times_k L]_d attached to it is \sum_j m_j[V_j] with the multiplicities coming from the associated cycle.

3c. Flat pullback of a cycle (Fulton's definition, valid since f is flat of relative dimension 0):
  f^*[W] = \sum_{j=1}^{r} \ell_j\,[V_j], \qquad \ell_j := \mathrm{length}_{\mathcal O_{W\times_k L,\,\xi_j}}\big(\mathcal O_{W\times_k L,\,\xi_j}\big).

3d. Proper pushforward of a cycle (f finite, hence proper): for each j the morphism V_j \to W is finite, surjective of degree [\kappa(\xi_j):\kappa(\eta)], so
  f_*[V_j] = [\kappa(\xi_j):K]\,[W].

3e. Arithmetic of the Artin algebra. Localising R\otimes_k L at S = R\setminus\{0\} gives
  A := S^{-1}(R\otimes_k L) \cong K\otimes_k L,
a K-algebra of dimension \dim_K A = \dim_k L = n; in particular A is Artinian. Its prime ideals are exactly the primes of R\otimes_k L disjoint from S, and since A is Artinian all of them are maximal and minimal; they are precisely p_1,\dots,p_r, the extensions of the generic points \xi_1,\dots,\xi_r. The structure theorem for Artinian rings gives A \cong \prod_{j=1}^{r} A_{p_j}, and each A_{p_j} is Artin local with residue field A/p_j = \kappa(\xi_j). Moreover A_{p_j} = (S^{-1}(R\otimes_k L))_{p_j} \cong \mathcal O_{W\times_k L,\xi_j}, so \mathrm{length}(A_{p_j}) = \ell_j. For an Artin local K-algebra (B,\mathfrak m,\kappa) one has \dim_K B = \mathrm{length}(B)\cdot[\kappa:K]: filter B \supset \mathfrak m \supset \cdots \supset \mathfrak m^{t}=0; each graded piece \mathfrak m^i/\mathfrak m^{i+1} is a \kappa-vector space, so \dim_K B = (\sum_i \dim_\kappa(\mathfrak m^i/\mathfrak m^{i+1}))\cdot[\kappa:K] = \mathrm{length}(B)\cdot[\kappa:K]. Summing over the product decomposition,
  n = \dim_K A = \sum_{j=1}^{r} \dim_K A_{p_j} = \sum_{j=1}^{r} \ell_j\,[\kappa(\xi_j):K].

3f. Combining 3c, 3d, 3e:
  f_* f^*[W] = \sum_j \ell_j\,[\kappa(\xi_j):K]\,[W] = \Big(\sum_j \ell_j[\kappa(\xi_j):K]\Big)[W] = n\,[W].
This proves the claim.

STEP 4. Extension to all cycles and to Chow groups.  Every Z \in Z_d(V) is a finite integral combination Z = \sum_i a_i[W_i] of integral closed d-dimensional subschemes, so by additivity of f^* and f_* on cycle groups and Step 3,
  f_* f^* Z = \sum_i a_i\, n [W_i] = n Z.
The flat pullback f^*: Z_d(V) \to Z_d(V_L) and the proper pushforward f_*: Z_d(V_L) \to Z_d(V) both carry rationally equivalent cycles to rationally equivalent cycles (functoriality of Chow groups for flat morphisms of relative dimension 0, and for proper morphisms), hence descend to homomorphisms on CH_d, and the identity f_*\circ f^* = n\cdot\mathrm{id} on Z_d descends to
  f_* f^* \alpha = n\,\alpha \qquad \text{for all } \alpha \in CH_d(V) = CH^d(X\times_k X).

STEP 5. Conclusion.  Let \alpha \in K = \ker(res). Identifying res with f^* via the isomorphism \phi of Step 1, res(\alpha) = f^*\alpha = 0 in CH^d(X_L\times_L X_L) \cong CH_d(V_L). Therefore, by Step 4,
  n\cdot\alpha = f_*(f^*\alpha) = f_*(0) = 0
in CH^d(X\times_k X), since f_* is a group homomorphism. This is exactly the assertion. (The cases n = 1, i.e. L = k, and d = 0 are covered by the same computation: a basis of L over k has n \ge 1 elements, and Steps 3a--3e only used that L is a non-zero free k-module of rank n.)

Remark on the role of the lemma: it shows that when L/k is finite the ideal K = \ker(CH^d(X\times X) \to CH^d(X_L\times X_L)) is annihilated by [L:k]; combined with a nilpotence statement for K\otimes \mathbb Q (or with the filtration-by-support argument used elsewhere in this development) it reduces the Rost nilpotence principle for arbitrary extensions to the case of a finite extension of the base field.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, and let p_{12}, p_{23}, p_{13}: X\times_k X\times_k X \to X\times_k X be the projections forgetting the third, first, and second factor. For closed subsets W, W' \subseteq X\times_k X set W \star W' = p_{13}(p_{12}^{-1}W \cap p_{23}^{-1}W'). If \alpha, \beta \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X\times_k X) are represented by cycles with supports in W and W' respectively, then the composite correspondence \alpha\circ\beta is represented by a cycle whose support lies in W \star W'.
proof:
Write $Y=X\times_k X$ and $T=X\times_k X\times_k X$, so $\dim Y=2d$ and $\dim T=3d$. Elements of $\mathrm{CH}^d(Y)$ are classes of $d$-dimensional cycles on $Y$. We use the standard convention for composition of correspondences
$$\alpha\circ\beta \;:=\; p_{13*}\bigl(p_{12}^{*}\alpha\;\cdot\;p_{23}^{*}\beta\bigr)\in \mathrm{CH}^{d}(Y),$$
where $\cdot$ is the intersection product on the smooth variety $T$, $p_{12}^*,p_{23}^*$ are flat pullbacks, and $p_{13*}$ is proper pushforward. (At the end we explain why the statement is independent of this convention.)

**Step 1: the three morphisms.** The projections $p_{12},p_{23},p_{13}\colon T\to Y$ are base changes of the structure morphism $X\to \operatorname{Spec}k$, hence smooth of relative dimension $d$; in particular they are flat, so flat pullback $p_{12}^*,p_{23}^*$ is defined on cycles and on Chow groups (Fulton, *Intersection Theory*, §1.7). Also $p_{13}$ is projective (a base change of $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, which is projective), hence proper, so proper pushforward $p_{13*}$ is defined. Since $T$ is smooth of dimension $3d$ over $k$, the diagonal $\Delta_T\hookrightarrow T\times_k T$ is a regular embedding of pure codimension $3d$.

**Step 2: the support property of the intersection product.** We use the following standard fact about refined Gysin homomorphisms (Fulton, *Intersection Theory*, §6.1 and §6.2): if $i\colon Z\hookrightarrow S$ is a regular embedding of pure codimension $c$ and $f\colon W\to S$ is any morphism, then $i^!\colon \mathrm{CH}_k W\to \mathrm{CH}_{k-c}(W\times_S Z)$ has the property that for every closed subscheme $V\subseteq W$ the class $i^![V]$ is represented by a cycle **on** $V\times_S W' = V\cap f^{-1}(Z)$ (it is the refined intersection product $Z\cdot V$, constructed from the normal cone $\mathcal{C}_{V\times_S Z}V$ by pulling back with the zero section $V\times_S Z\hookrightarrow \mathcal{C}_{V\times_S Z}V$; this construction is carried out inside $V\times_S Z$, so its cycle support lies there). By linearity, for any cycle $z=\sum n_jV_j$ on $W$ the cycle representing $i^!z$ is supported on $\bigcup_j (V_j\cap f^{-1}Z)=|z|\cap Z$.

Applying this with $S=W=T\times_k T$, $f=\mathrm{id}$, $i=\Delta_T\colon Z=\Delta_T\to T\times_k T$ (so $c=3d$), and using the definition of the product of cycles on the smooth variety $T$, namely $U\cdot V:=\Delta_T^!(U\times V)$ where $U\times V$ is the external product on $T\times T$, we obtain
$$\operatorname{Supp}(U\cdot V)\;\subseteq\;|U\times V|\cap \Delta_T \;=\; \operatorname{Supp}(U)\cap \operatorname{Supp}(V)\quad\text{(as a subset of }T\text{ via }\Delta_T\simeq T).$$
Here we used the elementary scheme-theoretic fact that for closed subschemes $F\subseteq T$, $F'\subseteq T$ the product $F\times_k F'\subseteq T\times_k T$ is defined by the ideal $\mathcal{I}_F\mathcal{O}_{T\times T}+\mathcal{I}_{F'}\mathcal{O}_{T\times T}$, hence $|F\times_k F'|=\mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}|F|\cap \mathrm{pr}_2^{-1}|F'|$, and therefore $\Delta_T\cap (F\times_k F')=F\cap F'$ set-theoretically.

**Step 3: choose representatives.** By hypothesis there are $d$-dimensional cycles $A,B$ on $Y$ with $[A]=\alpha$, $[B]=\beta$, $|A|:=\operatorname{Supp}(A)\subseteq W$ and $|B|:=\operatorname{Supp}(B)\subseteq W'$. (If $W=\varnothing$ or $W'=\varnothing$ then $A=0$ or $B=0$, hence $\alpha=0$ or $\beta=0$, so $\alpha\circ\beta=0$, which is represented by the zero cycle, supported on $\varnothing=W\star W'$; we may thus assume $A,B\neq 0$.)

**Step 4: supports after flat pullback.** Flat pullback of a cycle is nonzero and its support is the inverse image of the support (Fulton, §1.7: for a closed integral $V\subseteq Y$, $p_{12}^*[V]=[p_{12}^{-1}V]$, the scheme-theoretic inverse image, whose underlying set is $p_{12}^{-1}|V|$; same for $p_{23}$). Hence
$$|p_{12}^*A|=p_{12}^{-1}|A|\subseteq p_{12}^{-1}W,\qquad |p_{23}^*B|=p_{23}^{-1}|B|\subseteq p_{23}^{-1}W'.$$
Both are $2d$-dimensional cycles on $T$ (flat pullback preserves codimension: $p_{12}^{-1}|A|$ has dimension $d+d=2d$ in $T$, i.e. codimension $d$).

**Step 5: support of the product.** Set $F:=p_{12}^{-1}W\cap p_{23}^{-1}W'$, a closed subset of $T$. By Step 2 and Step 4,
$$\operatorname{Supp}\bigl(p_{12}^*A\cdot p_{23}^*B\bigr)\subseteq p_{12}^{-1}|A|\cap p_{23}^{-1}|B|\subseteq F.$$
The cycle $p_{12}^*A\cdot p_{23}^*B$ has dimension $2d+2d-3d=d$.

**Step 6: support after pushforward.** The proper pushforward of a cycle supported on a closed set $F$ is supported on the set-theoretic image $p_{13}(F)$: indeed $p_{13*}[C]=\deg(C/p_{13}(C))\,[p_{13}(C)]$ for each integral component $C$ of the cycle mapped onto a $d$-dimensional subvariety, and components whose image has dimension $<d$ are discarded; in either case every component of $p_{13*}C$ is of the form $p_{13}(C_i)$ with $C_i\subseteq F$. Thus
$$\operatorname{Supp}\bigl(p_{13*}(p_{12}^*A\cdot p_{23}^*B)\bigr)\subseteq p_{13}(F)=p_{13}\bigl(p_{12}^{-1}W\cap p_{23}^{-1}W'\bigr)=W\star W'.$$
(Since $p_{13}$ is proper and $F$ is closed, $W\star W'$ is in fact closed in $Y$.)

**Step 7: the class is $\alpha\circ\beta$.** The external product $\mathrm{CH}(T)\times\mathrm{CH}(T)\to\mathrm{CH}(T\times T)$ and the refined Gysin homomorphism $\Delta_T^!$ are both defined on rational-equivalence classes, and flat pullback and proper pushforward preserve rational equivalence. Hence the class of the cycle $p_{13*}(p_{12}^*A\cdot p_{23}^*B)$ is
$$p_{13*}\bigl(p_{12}^*[A]\cdot p_{23}^*[B]\bigr)=p_{13*}\bigl(p_{12}^*\alpha\cdot p_{23}^*\beta\bigr)=\alpha\circ\beta.$$
Combining Steps 6 and 7, $\alpha\circ\beta$ is represented by a cycle whose support lies in $W\star W'$, which is the claim.

**Step 8: independence of the convention (and a concrete description).** The product on $\mathrm{CH}(T)$ defined above by $\Delta_T^!$ coincides with the one obtained by moving to a proper intersection and using the Tor formula (Fulton, §1.6 and §6.2, or §17.4), so the argument does not depend on which of the two equivalent definitions of the Chow ring of a smooth variety one takes. Concretely, $W\star W'=\{(x_1,x_3)\in Y:\exists x_2\in X \text{ with } (x_1,x_2)\in W,\ (x_2,x_3)\in W'\}$. If instead one uses the opposite convention $\alpha\circ\beta=p_{13*}(p_{23}^*\alpha\cdot p_{12}^*\beta)$, the identical argument gives support in $p_{13}(p_{12}^{-1}W'\cap p_{23}^{-1}W)=W'\star W$; this is the transpose under the swap $\sigma\colon Y\to Y$, $(x_1,x_3)\mapsto(x_3,x_1)$, of the set obtained from $W\star W'$ by transposing $W,W'$, so the content of the lemma is unchanged. ∎

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let W \subseteq X\times_k X be a closed subset, and let p_1, p_2: X\times_k X \to X be the projections. Suppose there are closed subsets X = Z_0 \supseteq Z_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq Z_m = \emptyset such that p_2(p_1^{-1}(Z_j)\cap W) \subseteq Z_{j+1} for j = 0,\dots,m-1. Then every \alpha \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X\times_k X) that is represented by a cycle with support in W satisfies \alpha^{\circ m} = 0, the m-fold power for composition of correspondences.
proof:
Write $Y=X\times_k X$ and let $p_1,p_2:Y\to X$ be the two projections. We work with the underlying topological spaces; the support $\operatorname{Supp}(Z)$ of a cycle $Z$ on $Y$ is a Zariski-closed subset of $|Y|$, and all inclusions below are inclusions of subsets of $|Y|$ (equivalently, of the corresponding reduced closed subschemes).

**Step 0. The case $m=0$.** If $m=0$ the chain reads $X=Z_0=\emptyset$, so $X$ is the empty scheme, $Y=\emptyset$, $\mathrm{CH}^d(Y)=0$, hence $\alpha=0$; the $0$-fold power $\alpha^{\circ 0}$ is the class of the diagonal $\Delta_{\emptyset}=\emptyset\subset\emptyset\times\emptyset$, which is $0$. So the statement holds. In the sequel assume $m\ge 1$.

**Step 1. Reformulation of the hypothesis.** For $j=0,\dots,m-1$ we claim
$$
(\ast)\qquad W\cap p_1^{-1}(Z_j)\ \subseteq\ p_2^{-1}(Z_{j+1}).
$$
Indeed, let $(x,y)\in W\cap p_1^{-1}(Z_j)$, i.e. $x\in Z_j$ and $(x,y)\in W$. Then $y=p_2(x,y)\in p_2\bigl(W\cap p_1^{-1}(Z_j)\bigr)\subseteq Z_{j+1}$ by hypothesis, so $(x,y)\in p_2^{-1}(Z_{j+1})$.

**Step 2. The star product, set-theoretically.** For closed subsets $A,B\subseteq Y$ put $A\star B=p_{13}(p_{12}^{-1}A\cap p_{23}^{-1}B)$ as in lemma_58, where $p_{12},p_{23},p_{13}:X^3\to Y$ forget the third, first, and second factor. Unwinding the definitions, for $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in X^3$ we have $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in p_{12}^{-1}A\cap p_{23}^{-1}B$ iff $(x_1,x_2)\in A$ and $(x_2,x_3)\in B$. Hence, purely set-theoretically,
$$
(\dagger)\qquad (x,z)\in A\star B\iff \exists\,y\in X\ \text{with}\ (x,y)\in A\ \text{and}\ (y,z)\in B .
$$

**Step 3. The iterated supports.** Define closed subsets $S_1,\dots,S_m\subseteq Y$ by
$$S_1=W,\qquad S_{n+1}=W\star S_n\quad (1\le n\le m-1).$$

**Claim.** For all integers $n\ge 1$ and $j\ge 0$ with $n+j\le m$,
$$
S_n\cap p_1^{-1}(Z_j)\ \subseteq\ p_2^{-1}(Z_{n+j}).
$$

*Proof of the claim*, by induction on $n$.

- $n=1$: $S_1=W$ and $1+j\le m$ gives $j\le m-1$, so this is exactly $(\ast)$ with $n+j=j+1$.

- Inductive step: let $n\ge 1$ and suppose the claim holds at level $n$ (for every admissible $j$). Take $j\ge 0$ with $(n+1)+j\le m$, and let $(x,z)\in S_{n+1}\cap p_1^{-1}(Z_j)$, so $x\in Z_j$. By $(\dagger)$ applied to $S_{n+1}=W\star S_n$ there is $y\in X$ with $(x,y)\in W$ and $(y,z)\in S_n$. Since $(x,y)\in W\cap p_1^{-1}(Z_j)$, $(\ast)$ (which applies because $j\le m-1$) gives $y\in Z_{j+1}$. Thus $(y,z)\in S_n\cap p_1^{-1}(Z_{j+1})$, and since $n+(j+1)=(n+1)+j\le m$ the induction hypothesis at level $n$ and index $j+1$ yields $z\in Z_{n+j+1}=Z_{(n+1)+j}$. Hence $(x,z)\in p_2^{-1}(Z_{(n+1)+j})$, proving the claim at level $n+1$. $\square$

**Step 4. $S_m$ is empty.** Apply the claim with $n=m$, $j=0$ (note $m+0\le m$). Since $Z_0=X$, $p_1^{-1}(Z_0)=Y$, so $S_m=S_m\cap Y\subseteq p_2^{-1}(Z_m)=p_2^{-1}(\emptyset)=\emptyset$. Thus $S_m=\emptyset$.

**Step 5. Supports of the powers of $\alpha$.** We show by induction on $n$ that $\alpha^{\circ n}$ (the $n$-fold composite correspondence; composition is associative, so the parenthesisation is irrelevant) is represented by a cycle on $Y$ whose support lies in $S_n$.

- $n=1$: by hypothesis $\alpha$ is represented by a cycle $Z$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(Z)\subseteq W=S_1$.

- Inductive step: assume $\alpha^{\circ n}$ is represented by a cycle $Z_n$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(Z_n)\subseteq S_n$. Since $\alpha^{\circ(n+1)}=\alpha\circ\alpha^{\circ n}$, we may apply lemma_58 to the two classes $\alpha$ (represented by $Z$, support in $W$) and $\beta=\alpha^{\circ n}$ (represented by $Z_n$, support in $S_n$): the composite $\alpha\circ\alpha^{\circ n}$ is represented by a cycle whose support lies in $W\star S_n=S_{n+1}$.

Taking $n=m$, $\alpha^{\circ m}$ is represented by a cycle whose support lies in $S_m=\emptyset$. A cycle with empty support has no irreducible components, i.e. it is the zero cycle. Therefore $\alpha^{\circ m}=0$ in $\mathrm{CH}^d(X\times_k X)$.

This completes the proof. (Note that the only property of $X$ used beyond smooth projectivity — which is needed for the correspondence product to be defined and for lemma_58 — is the set-theoretic behaviour of the supports; no properness beyond what lemma_58 requires is used, and the argument is valid for integral coefficients.)

statement: Let $Y$ be a smooth variety over a field $k$, let $M=Y\times_k\mathbb{A}^1_k$, and let $s:Y\to M$ be the zero section. For a closed point $t\in\mathbb{A}^1_k$ with residue field $\kappa(t)$, let $i_t:Y\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t)\to M$ be the induced closed immersion. Then for every $n\ge 0$ and every $\beta\in\mathrm{CH}^{n-1}(Y\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t))$ with integral coefficients, the refined Gysin pullback of $i_{t*}\beta$ along the regular embedding $s$ vanishes: $s^{!}(i_{t*}\beta)=0$ in $\mathrm{CH}^{n}(Y)$.
proof:
We work with integral coefficients throughout. Write $\mathbb A^1_k=\operatorname{Spec} k[u]$, let $0\in\mathbb A^1_k$ denote the origin (the closed point with ideal $(u)$, residue field $k$), and let $t\in\mathbb A^1_k$ be a closed point; then the ideal of $t$ in $k[u]$ is generated by a unique monic irreducible polynomial $f$, and $\kappa(t)=k[u]/(f)$. Put $Y_t:=Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)$ and $D:=s(Y)\subset M$.

If $Y=\varnothing$ then $M=\varnothing$ and all Chow groups involved are $0$, so assume $Y\neq\varnothing$ and let $m=\dim Y$; then $\dim M=m+1$. If $n=0$ then $\beta\in\mathrm{CH}^{-1}(Y_t)=0$, so there is nothing to prove; assume $n\ge 1$.

**Step 1: $D$ and $Y_t$ are effective Cartier divisors of $M$, and $\mathcal O_M(D)$ is trivial.**
Cover $M$ by affine opens $W\times\mathbb A^1$ with $W=\operatorname{Spec} A\subset Y$ affine; then $\mathcal O_M(W\times\mathbb A^1)=A[u]$. Both $u$ and $f$ are monic polynomials in $A[u]$, and a monic polynomial is a non-zero-divisor over any ring: if $a(u)=\sum_{i\le d}a_i u^i\ne0$ with $a_d\ne0$ and $h(u)$ is monic of degree $e$ with leading coefficient $1$, then $a\cdot h$ has leading coefficient $a_d\cdot 1=a_d\ne0$, hence $a\cdot h\ne0$. Thus $u$ and $f$ are non-zero-divisors on every affine open of $M$, so $(u)\mathcal O_M$ and $(f)\mathcal O_M$ are invertible ideal sheaves; their zero schemes are
$$Z(u)=Y\times_k\{0\}=s(Y)=D,\qquad Z(f)=Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)=Y_t,$$
by definition of $s$ and $i_t$ as base changes of $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\mathbb A^1$ and $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)\to\mathbb A^1$. Hence $s$ and $i_t$ are regular embeddings of pure codimension $1$; in particular $i_{t*}:\mathrm{CH}^{n-1}(Y_t)\to\mathrm{CH}^{n}(M)$ (and $s$ identifies $\mathrm{CH}^{n}(Y)$ with $\mathrm{CH}_{m-n}(D)$).
Triviality of $\mathcal O_M(D)$: multiplication by $u$ gives an isomorphism $\mathcal O_M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathcal I_D=u\mathcal O_M$ (injective since $u$ is a non-zero-divisor, surjective by definition of $\mathcal I_D$). Thus $\mathcal O_M(-D)=\mathcal I_D\simeq\mathcal O_M$, and dualising, $\mathcal O_M(D)=\mathcal{H}om(\mathcal I_D,\mathcal O_M)\simeq\mathcal O_M$; explicitly $1\in\mathcal O_M$ maps to the $\mathcal O_M$-linear endomorphism $u\cdot a\mapsto a$ of $\mathcal I_D$, which is well defined because $u$ is a non-zero-divisor. So $\mathcal O_M(D)$ is the trivial line bundle (as it must be: $D$ is the zero scheme of a global function, i.e. a principal Cartier divisor). Consequently the normal bundle $N_{Y/M}=\mathcal O_M(D)|_D$ is also trivial.

**Step 2: The Cartier-divisor model of the refined Gysin homomorphism (standard description; no moving involved).**
Let $i:H\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an effective Cartier divisor, locally $H=Z(g)$ with $g$ a non-zero-divisor, and let $i^!:\mathrm{CH}_k(X)\to\mathrm{CH}_{k-1}(H)$ be the refined Gysin homomorphism of the regular embedding $i$. For an integral closed subscheme $V\subset X$ of dimension $k$ one has:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] if $V\not\subset H$, then $i^![V]$ is the class in $\mathrm{CH}_{k-1}(H)$ of the cycle associated with the Cartier divisor $H|_V$ on $V$, namely $\sum_{\xi\in V^{(1)}}\ell_{\mathcal O_{V,\xi}}(\mathcal O_{V,\xi}/(g))\,[\overline\xi]$, a cycle supported on $V\cap H$;
\item[(b)] if $V\subset H$, then $i^![V]=c_1(\mathcal O_X(H)|_V)\cap[V]\in\mathrm{CH}_{k-1}(V)$, viewed in $\mathrm{CH}_{k-1}(H)$ by push-forward.
\end{itemize}
These formulas are additive on cycles and respect rational equivalence, hence define $i^!$. This is the standard description of the refined Gysin homomorphism in codimension one (Fulton, *Intersection Theory*, \S2.3 for the operation "intersect with a Cartier divisor", and Example 8.1.7 for its identification with $i^!$; (b) is the excess/self-intersection formula for a Cartier divisor). It is the form in which $i^!$ is often defined in codimension $1$; in particular, unlike the general regular-embedding case, no moving of cycles is needed. We apply this with $i=s$, $H=D$, $X=M$.

**Step 3: Reduction to integral components.**
Choose a cycle representative $\sum_j n_jV_j$ of $\beta$, with each $V_j\subset Y_t$ integral of codimension $n-1$ in $Y_t$ (equivalently of codimension $n$ in $M$, since $Y_t$ is an effective Cartier divisor). Then $\sum_j n_j[V_j]$ is a cycle representative of $i_{t*}\beta$ on $M$ (each $V_j$ is closed in $M$ because $Y_t$ is closed in $M$). By additivity of $s^!$ on Chow groups (Step 2), $s^!(i_{t*}\beta)=\sum_j n_j\,s^![V_j]$, so it suffices to prove $s^![V_j]=0$ for every $j$.

**Step 4: Case $t\neq 0$.**
Here $t$ is a closed point distinct from the origin, so the maximal ideals $(f)\ne(u)$ of $k[u]$. Writing $f=q\,u+f(0)$ with $q\in k[u]$ and $f(0)\in k^{\times}$ (as $f\ne u$ is irreducible, $u\nmid f$, i.e. $f(0)\ne0$), we get $1=f(0)^{-1}(f-qu)\in(f,u)$, so $k[u]/(f,u)=0$. Hence
$$Y_t\cap D \;=\; Y\times_k\bigl(\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)\times_{\mathbb A^1}\operatorname{Spec}k\bigr)=Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(k[u]/(f,u)\bigr)=\varnothing .$$
Thus each $V_j\subset Y_t$ satisfies $V_j\cap D=\varnothing$, and since $V_j\ne\varnothing$ also $V_j\not\subset D$. By Step 2(a), $s^![V_j]$ is the class of the cycle of the Cartier divisor $D|_{V_j}$, which is cut out on $V_j$ by $\bar u:=u|_{V_j}\in\Gamma(V_j,\mathcal O_{V_j})$. The equality $V_j\cap Z(\bar u)=V_j\cap D=\varnothing$ says that the image of $\bar u$ in $\kappa(w)$ is non-zero for every point $w\in V_j$; a regular function on a scheme whose image in every residue field is non-zero is a unit (its stalk at each point lies outside the maximal ideal, so multiplication by it is a stalkwise isomorphism). Hence $\bar u\in\Gamma(V_j,\mathcal O_{V_j})^{\times}$, i.e. $D|_{V_j}$ is the trivial Cartier divisor. For every codimension-one point $\xi$ of $V_j$ the element $\bar u$ is a unit of the discrete valuation ring $\mathcal O_{V_j,\xi}$, so $\mathcal O_{V_j,\xi}/(\bar u)=0$ and $\ell_{\mathcal O_{V_j,\xi}}(\mathcal O_{V_j,\xi}/(\bar u))=0$. The associated cycle is therefore the zero cycle, and $s^![V_j]=0$ in $\mathrm{CH}_{m-n}(D)$.

**Step 5: Case $t=0$.**
Then the ideal of $t$ is $(u)$, so $f=u$, $\kappa(t)=k$, $Y_t=Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}k=Y$, and $i_t=s$; in particular $\beta\in\mathrm{CH}^{n-1}(Y)$. Each $V_j$ is an integral closed subscheme of $M$ contained in $D$. By Step 2(b),
$$s^![V_j]=c_1\bigl(\mathcal O_M(D)|_{V_j}\bigr)\cap[V_j]\in\mathrm{CH}_{m-n}(V_j)\subset \mathrm{CH}_{m-n}(D).$$
By Step 1, $\mathcal O_M(D)\simeq\mathcal O_M$, so $\mathcal O_M(D)|_{V_j}\simeq\mathcal O_{V_j}$ is trivial. The first Chern class of a trivial line bundle acts by zero: by definition $c_1(L)\cap\alpha=D'\cdot\alpha$ for any Cartier divisor $D'$ with $\mathcal O(D')\simeq L$, and for $L=\mathcal O_{V_j}$ we may take $D'=\mathrm{div}(1)$, the trivial Cartier divisor, whose local equations are units, so that $D'|_W$ is the trivial Cartier divisor on every subvariety $W$ and $D'\cdot[W]=0$; hence $c_1(\mathcal O_{V_j})\cap[V_j]=0$. (Equivalently: $c_1$ factors through $\mathrm{Pic}$, and the trivial bundle represents $0$.) Thus $s^![V_j]=0$. Concretely this is the self-intersection formula $s^!s_*\beta=c_1(N_{Y/M})\cap\beta$ with $N_{Y/M}$ trivial.

**Step 6: Conclusion.**
In both cases $s^![V_j]=0$ for every $j$, whence $s^!(i_{t*}\beta)=\sum_j n_j\cdot 0=0$ in $\mathrm{CH}_{m-n}(D)=\mathrm{CH}^{n}(Y)$. The value obtained is independent of the chosen representative because $s^!$ is a well-defined homomorphism on Chow groups (Step 2). This proves the lemma for every $n\ge0$, every closed point $t\in\mathbb A^1_k$, and every $\beta\in\mathrm{CH}^{n-1}(Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)$).

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d with projections p_1, p_2: X x X -> X, and let alpha, beta in CH^d(X x X). Suppose alpha has a d-dimensional cycle representative supported on C x D and beta has a d-dimensional cycle representative supported on C' x D', where C, D, C', D' are closed subschemes of X. Then alpha o beta, the composition of correspondences, has a d-dimensional cycle representative supported on C x D' all of whose integral components Z_i satisfy dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i <= dim C + dim D'.
proof:
PROOF OF lemma_54.

=== Conventions ===
Write Y = X ×ₖ X and X³ = X ×ₖ X ×ₖ X; let p₁₂, p₂₃, p₁₃ : X³ → Y be the projections forgetting the third, the first, and the second factor respectively. Composition of correspondences is taken in the convention used throughout this development (cf. lemma_33_2, lemma_36):
    (∗)   α∘β := p₁₃∗( p₁₂^*α · p₂₃^*β )  in CH^d(Y),
where · is the intersection product on the smooth variety X³ and p₁₃∗ the proper pushforward (proper because X is projective over k). Since X is smooth of dimension d, dim Y = 2d and dim X³ = 3d, so a class of CH^d(Y) is the class of a d-dimensional cycle on Y, and a class of CH^{2d}(X³) is the class of a d-dimensional cycle on X³. For a cycle σ, |σ| = Supp(σ). For a closed subscheme T of a variety we write |T| for its underlying closed subset and dim T := dim|T|; "σ is supported on T" means |σ| ⊆ |T|. Images and intersections of closed subsets below are always set-theoretic.

=== Step 1. The input data ===
By hypothesis there are d-dimensional cycles A and B on Y with [A] = α, [B] = β and
    |A| ⊆ |C| × |D| ⊆ Y,      |B| ⊆ |C'| × |D'| ⊆ Y.
(If A = 0 or B = 0 then (∗) gives α∘β = 0 by bilinearity of the product, and the conclusion is vacuous; we may and do assume both are non-zero, which forces dim C + dim D ≥ d and dim C' + dim D' ≥ d.)

=== Step 2. Support containment, via the proved lemma_58 ===
Apply lemma_58 to the closed subsets W := |C| × |D| and W' := |C'| × |D'| of Y. Since α, β are represented by cycles with supports in W, W' respectively, lemma_58 yields that α∘β is represented by a d-dimensional cycle Z on Y whose support lies in
    W ⋆ W' := p₁₃( p₁₂^{-1}W ∩ p₂₃^{-1}W' ).
We compute the three sets explicitly:
  • p₁₂^{-1}W = { (x₁,x₂,x₃) ∈ X³ : (x₁,x₂) ∈ |C|×|D| } = |C| × |D| × |X|;
  • p₂₃^{-1}W' = { (x₁,x₂,x₃) ∈ X³ : (x₂,x₃) ∈ |C'|×|D'| } = |X| × |C'| × |D'|;
  • their intersection is |C| × (|D| ∩ |C'|) × |D'|, since the first and third conditions are x₁ ∈ |C| and x₃ ∈ |D'| and the middle condition is x₂ ∈ |D| ∩ |C'|;
  • p₁₃( |C| × (|D|∩|C'|) × |D'| ) = { (x₁,x₃) : x₁ ∈ |C|, x₃ ∈ |D'|, and |D|∩|C'| ≠ ∅ } ⊆ |C| × |D'|; it is empty exactly when |D| ∩ |C'| = ∅, and equals |C|×|D'| otherwise.
Hence W ⋆ W' ⊆ |C| × |D'|, and α∘β has a d-dimensional cycle representative Z with |Z| ⊆ |C| × |D'|. (Step 5 re-derives this directly, with the sharper intermediate support |C| × (|D|∩|C'|) × |D'| before the pushforward by p₁₃, so that the input being used is fully visible.)

=== Step 3. The numerical bound on the components ===
Write Z = Σᵢ nᵢ Zᵢ with the Zᵢ distinct integral closed subschemes of Y of dimension d and nᵢ ∈ ℤ \ {0}; these are the integral components of the representative Z. Each Zᵢ is contained in |C| × |D'|. The morphism Zᵢ → X (restriction of p₁) has closed image, because Zᵢ is closed in Y = X ×ₖ X with X projective over k, hence Zᵢ is proper over k, and the image of a proper scheme under a k-morphism is closed. Moreover
    p₁(Zᵢ) ⊆ p₁(|C| × |D'|) = |C|,        p₂(Zᵢ) ⊆ p₂(|C| × |D'|) = |D'|.
A closed subset of |C| has dimension at most dim C, and similarly for D'; therefore
    dim p₁ Zᵢ ≤ dim C   and   dim p₂ Zᵢ ≤ dim D',
and adding these two inequalities gives, for every i,
    dim p₁ Zᵢ + dim p₂ Zᵢ ≤ dim C + dim D'.
This is precisely the estimate required in the statement, and Z is the required d-dimensional cycle representative supported on C × D'.

=== Step 4. Edge and vanishing cases ===
• If |D| ∩ |C'| = ∅, then W ⋆ W' = ∅, so Z = 0 and α∘β = 0. The empty cycle is a d-dimensional representative supported on C × D' with no integral components, so the assertion holds vacuously.
• If dim C + dim D' < d, then dim(C × D') = dim C + dim D' < d (dimension of a product of schemes of finite type over a field is the sum of the dimensions), so |C| × |D'| contains no integral closed subscheme of dimension d; the representative Z of Step 2 must therefore be 0, and again α∘β = 0 and the componentwise inequality is vacuous. (This is consistent with the convention lev(0) = −1 of lemma_44; we do not need to state any inequality for the empty maximum.)
• If C = ∅ or D' = ∅ the same vacuity applies.
Thus in all cases the conclusion of the lemma holds.

=== Step 5. Direct justification of the support mechanism used in Step 2 ===
We spell out why the containment in Step 2 is true, using only standard properties of refined Gysin homomorphisms (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Ch. 1 and Ch. 6). This is the content of the already-proved lemma_58; we record the argument because it exhibits the sharper intermediate support.

Standard facts used:
 (F1) Flat pullback of cycles (I.1.7(a)): for a flat morphism f of relative dimension e, f^*[V] = [f^{-1}V] and f^* respects rational equivalence.
 (F2) Product on a smooth variety via the diagonal (I.8.1/6.2): if M is smooth of dimension m with diagonal δ_M : M → M × M (a regular embedding of codimension m), then u·v = δ_M^!(u × v), where u × v is the exterior product of cycles/classes on M × M.
 (F3) Existence of the refined Gysin homomorphism for an arbitrary cartesian square (I, Ch. 6 §1, p. 98): given a cartesian square
        S' --q--> S
         |        |
         v   g    v f
        M' -----> M
     in which f : S → M is a regular embedding of codimension c, there is a homomorphism f^! = g_{S'}^! : CH_r(S) → CH_{r−c}(S'). No regularity whatever is assumed of the base change q; that is precisely the point of the refined construction.
 (F4) Compatibility of refined Gysin with proper pushforward (I.6.2(a)): in the situation of (F3), if g is proper then f^!(g_* a) = q_*? — more precisely, with the notation of (F3) and with g proper,  f^!(g_* a) = g'_*(f^! a), where g' : S' → M' is the base change of g.
 (F5) Support of a proper pushforward of a cycle (I.1.4): for proper h : P → Q and a cycle Σ n_j[V_j] on P, h_*Σ n_j[V_j] is the cycle Σ n_j d_j [h(V_j)] with d_j ≥ 0, omitting (i.e. giving coefficient 0 to) those V_j with dim h(V_j) < dim V_j; in particular its support is contained in h(|σ|).

5a. Pull the representatives back to X³. p₁₂ : X³ → Y is smooth of relative dimension d, hence flat; by (F1), p₁₂^*[A] = [A × X], a 2d-dimensional cycle on X³ with support p₁₂^{-1}|A| ⊆ |C| × |D| × |X|. Likewise p₂₃^*[B] = [X × B], a 2d-dimensional cycle with support ⊆ |X| × |C'| × |D'|.

5b. Exterior product. By (F2), p₁₂^*α · p₂₃^*β = δ^!( (p₁₂^*[A]) × (p₂₃^*[B]) ) in CH(X³), where δ = δ_{X³} : X³ → X³ × X³ = X⁶ is the diagonal, a regular embedding of codimension m = 3d, and where the exterior product is the 4d-dimensional cycle
        Σ := (A × X) × (X × B)  on  X⁶,
whose support is contained in |C| × |D| × |X| × |C'| × |D'| =: |S|, with S the closed subscheme (C × D × X) × (X × C' × D') of X⁶ = (X³) × (X³). Thus p₁₂^*α · p₂₃^*β = δ^!(g_*γ), where g : S → X⁶ is the closed immersion, γ ∈ Z_{4d}(S) is the cycle Σ viewed on S, and r := 4d = dim-relevant degree, so that r − m = 4d − 3d = d.

5c. The support claim. Form the cartesian square
        S_δ --q--> S
         | j       | g
         v         v
        X³ --δ--> X⁶,
where S_δ := S ×_{X⁶} X³ and j is the base change of the closed immersion g, hence itself a closed immersion (in particular proper). Nothing is asserted about q: by (F3) the regular embedding δ of codimension m determines a homomorphism δ_S^! : CH_r(S) → CH_{r−m}(S_δ) for this square, with no hypothesis on q. By (F4), applied to the same square (g is proper),
        δ^!(g_*γ) = j_*( δ_S^! γ )   in  CH_{r−m}(X³) = CH_d(X³).
Now δ_S^!γ is by definition represented by a cycle Γ on the scheme S_δ, so |Γ| ⊆ |S_δ|; by (F5) the pushforward j_*Γ is a cycle on X³ whose support is contained in j(|S_δ|). Since the map on underlying topological spaces of a fibre product is surjective onto the set-theoretic fibre product, j(|S_δ|) = δ^{-1}(|S|) = { x ∈ X³ : (x,x) ∈ |S| }. This proves: δ^!(g_*γ) is represented by a d-dimensional cycle W on X³ with |W| ⊆ δ^{-1}(|S|). (If r − m < 0 then CH_{r−m}(S_δ) = 0 and the product is 0, so the statement is vacuous; here r − m = d ≥ 0.)

5d. Evaluate δ^{-1}(|S|). A point (x₁,x₂,x₃) ∈ X³ lies in δ^{-1}(|S|) iff (x₁,x₂,x₃) ∈ |C|×|D|×|X| and (x₁,x₂,x₃) ∈ |X|×|C'|×|D'|, i.e. iff x₁ ∈ |C|, x₂ ∈ |D| ∩ |C'|, x₃ ∈ |D'|. Hence
        δ^{-1}(|S|) = |C| × (|D| ∩ |C'|) × |D'|,
so p₁₂^*α · p₂₃^*β is represented by a d-dimensional cycle W with |W| ⊆ |C| × (|D|∩|C'|) × |D'|. We deliberately assert nothing more about W: it is in general NOT the naive fibre-product cycle A ×_X B, because the square involved need not be transverse and excess-intersection contributions occur; only the support containment is used.

5e. Push forward by p₁₃.   "proof": "PROOF OF lemma_63.

Setup. Let k be a field, let A be a k-algebra which is an integral domain and finitely generated as a k-algebra, and let 0 \neq f \in A. We must produce a field E, finite over k, and a k-algebra homomorphism \varphi: A \to E with \varphi(f) \neq 0.

Remark on the earlier (rejected) attempt: that proof tried to deduce Zariski's lemma from Noether normalization via the substitution z_i = y_i - y_m^{N^{i-1}} (1 \le i \le m-1), z_m = y_m, whose z_m-weights \alpha_m + \sum_{i<m}\alpha_i N^{i-1} are not distinct (the monomials T_1 and T_m both have weight 1), so the top-weight coefficient need not be a constant and no monic relation is obtained (e.g. P = T_1 - T_m becomes z_1). Below we do not use Noether normalization at all; we give a direct, self-contained proof of Zariski's lemma (Claim 4) via a localization/integrality argument, so the flaw cannot recur. The only non-constructive input is Zorn's lemma.

=====================================================================
CLAIM 1 (the localization A \hookrightarrow A_f). Put B := A[T]/(fT-1), let \iota: A \to B be the composition A \to A[T] \twoheadrightarrow B, and let \tau \in B be the class of T. Then:
(i) \iota(f)\tau = 1 in B, so \iota(f) is a unit of B;
(ii) \iota is injective, hence B \neq 0;
(iii) B is a finitely generated k-algebra.

Proof. (i) is immediate from the relation fT - 1 = 0 in the quotient.
(ii) Suppose a \in A maps to 0 in B, i.e. a = (fT-1)h(T) in A[T] for some h = \sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j T^j with d_j \in A. Expanding, (fT-1)h = -d_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{m}(f d_{j-1} - d_j)T^j + f d_m T^{m+1}. Comparing with the constant polynomial a gives -d_0 = a, d_j = f d_{j-1} = -f^{j}a for 1 \le j \le m, and 0 = f d_m = -f^{m+1} a. Since A is a domain and f \neq 0, also f^{m+1} \neq 0; hence a = 0. So \ker\iota = 0. As an integral domain A is nonzero (1 \neq 0), so B \neq 0.
(iii) Write A = k[a_1,\dots,a_s]. Every element of B is the class of some \sum_{j=0}^{n} c_j T^j with c_j \in A, i.e. equals \sum_j \iota(c_j)\tau^j; each c_j is a polynomial in the a_i, so B is generated as a ring over k by \iota(a_1),\dots,\iota(a_s),\tau. \square

=====================================================================
CLAIM 2 (a maximal ideal avoiding f). There is a maximal ideal \mathfrak n \subsetneq B, and E := B/\mathfrak n is a field which is a finitely generated k-algebra, such that the composite \varphi: A \xrightarrow{\ \iota\ } B \twoheadrightarrow E satisfies \varphi(f) \neq 0.

Proof. The set \mathcal I of proper ideals of B is nonempty: (0) is proper because B \neq 0 (Claim 1(ii)). If (I_\lambda) is a chain in \mathcal I, then I := \bigcup_\lambda I_\lambda is an ideal (sums and multiples land in the largest of the two members of the chain), and I is proper: if 1 \in I then 1 \in I_\lambda for some \lambda, contradicting I_\lambda \in \mathcal I. Thus (\mathcal I,\subseteq) is inductively ordered, and Zorn's lemma yields a maximal element \mathfrak n. Since B is commutative with 1, E := B/\mathfrak n is a field. Let q: B \twoheadrightarrow E be the quotient map, which is unital; q sends the unit \iota(f) of B to a unit of E, and a unit of a nonzero ring is nonzero, so q(\iota(f)) \neq 0. Thus \varphi := q \circ \iota satisfies \varphi(f) \neq 0. Finally E is a quotient of the finitely generated k-algebra B (Claim 1(iii)), hence is itself a finitely generated k-algebra. \square

By Claims 1-2 the lemma follows once we prove:

=====================================================================
CLAIM 3 (auxiliary elementary facts).

(3a) Euclid's argument: k[T] has infinitely many pairwise non-associate irreducible polynomials. Indeed, if p_1,\dots,p_s were all of them (up to associates), the polynomial P := p_1\cdots p_s + 1 has degree \ge 1, so P is a nonzero nonunit; factoring P (which terminates by strict decrease of degrees: if a nonzero nonunit is not irreducible, split it into two factors of strictly smaller positive degree and repeat) gives an irreducible divisor q of P. Then q is not associate to any p_i, for p_i \mid P and p_i \mid p_1\cdots p_s would give p_i \mid 1. Contradiction.

(3b) Let p \in k[t_1] be irreducible. Since k[t_1] is a Euclidean domain, p is prime there: if p \mid ab with p \nmid a, then gcd(p,a) = 1 (the only divisors of the irreducible p are units and associates), and B\'ezout's identity (Euclidean algorithm) gives up + va = 1, hence p \mid b. Moreover, for every r \ge 1, p is a prime element of R := k[t_1,\dots,t_r]: indeed R/(p) \cong (k[t_1]/(p))[t_2,\dots,t_r] (the map S[x_2,\dots,x_r] \to (S/(p))[x_2,\dots,x_r] for S = k[t_1] is surjective with kernel (p)), and k[t_1]/(p) is a field because (p) is maximal in the PID k[t_1] (any ideal strictly containing (p) is generated by a proper divisor of p, hence is k[t_1]). Thus R/(p) is a domain, i.e. (p) is a prime ideal of R.

(3c) Let r \ge 1, R = k[t_1,\dots,t_r], and 0 \neq g \in R. Then S := R[1/g] \subset \mathrm{Frac}(R) is NOT a field. Write g = \sum_{\mu} C_\mu(t_1)\, t_2^{\mu_2}\cdots t_r^{\mu_r} as a polynomial in t_2,\dots,t_r with coefficients C_\mu \in k[t_1]; the representation is unique since the monomials t_2^{\mu_2}\cdots t_r^{\mu_r} form a free k[t_1]-basis of R = k[t_1][t_2,\dots,t_r]. Some C_\mu is nonzero; fix one and call it C. The nonzero polynomial C has only finitely many irreducible divisors (up to associates), so by (3a) there is an irreducible p \in k[t_1] with p \nmid C. Then p \nmid g in R: if g = p h with h = \sum_\mu H_\mu(t_1) t_2^{\mu_2}\cdots t_r^{\mu_r}, comparing coefficients gives C_\mu = p H_\mu for every \mu, in particular p \mid C, contradiction. Since R is a domain and g \neq 0, the map R \to S is injective and the elements of S are exactly the fractions h/g^m (h \in R, m \ge 0), with equality computed in \mathrm{Frac}(R). The element p \in R maps to a nonzero element of S. If S were a field, 1/p \in S, so 1/p = h/g^m in \mathrm{Frac}(R), i.e. g^m = p h in R, i.e. p \mid g^m; by primeness of p in R (3b), p \mid g, contradiction. Hence S is not a field.

(3d) Determinant trick. Let C be a ring, B \subseteq C a subring, and suppose C = \sum_{i=1}^{s} B\omega_i is generated by s elements as B-module. Then every c \in C is integral over B. Proof: write c\omega_i = \sum_j b_{ij}\omega_j with b_{ij} \in B, and set M := (c\delta_{ij} - b_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le s} \in M_s(C). Then M acts on the column vector (\omega_1,\dots,\omega_s)^t as 0, so by Cramer's rule \det(M)\,\omega_i = 0 for all i (each \det(M)\omega_i is the i-th component of \mathrm{adj}(M)\cdot M\cdot\omega = 0). Writing 1 = \sum_i \beta_i\omega_i with \beta_i \in B (possible since the \omega_i generate C as B-module), we get \det(M) = \det(M)\cdot 1 = \sum_i \beta_i \det(M)\omega_i = 0. Expanding \det(cI - (b_{ij})) shows that c satisfies the monic polynomial \det(T I - (b_{ij})) \in B[T], which is monic of degree s. \square

(3e) If B \subseteq E with E a field and E a finitely generated B-module, then B is a field. Proof: by (3d) E is integral over B. For 0 \neq b \in B, the element b^{-1} \in E satisfies (b^{-1})^m + c_{m-1}(b^{-1})^{m-1} + \dots + c_0 = 0 with c_i \in B and m \ge 1; multiplying by b^{m-1} gives b^{-1} = -(c_{m-1} + c_{m-2}b + \dots + c_0 b^{m-1}) \in B. So every nonzero element of B is invertible in B.

(3f) Transcendence basis for finitely generated field extensions. If \Omega/k is a field extension generated by x_1,\dots,x_n \in \Omega, then there are indices 1 \le i_1 < \dots < i_r \le n such that t_1 := x_{i_1},\dots,t_r := x_{i_r} are algebraically independent over k and \Omega is algebraic over k(t_1,\dots,t_r). Proof by induction on n: n = 0 is trivial. For n \ge 1, by induction there are t_1,\dots,t_r among x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}, algebraically independent over k, with K := k(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}) algebraic over k(t_1,\dots,t_r). Then \Omega = K(x_n) is algebraic over k(t_1,\dots,t_r)(x_n), because each x_i (i \le n-1) is algebraic over k(t_1,\dots,t_r), hence a fortiori over the larger field k(t_1,\dots,t_r)(x_n). If x_n is transcendental over k(t_1,\dots,t_r), then t_1,\dots,t_r,x_n are algebraically independent and \Omega is algebraic over k(t_1,\dots,t_r,x_n): done. If x_n is algebraic over k(t_1,\dots,t_r), then \Omega is algebraic over k(t_1,\dots,t_r) as well, using that "algebraic over algebraic is algebraic": indeed, if a \in \Omega is algebraic over a field F which is algebraic over k, and a satisfies T^m + \kappa_{m-1}T^{m-1} + \dots + \kappa_0 \in F[T], then k(\kappa_0,\dots,\kappa_{m-1}) is a finite k-vector space (it is generated by finitely many algebraic elements, and F[a'] for a' algebraic over a field F' is spanned by 1,a',\dots,a'^{\deg-1}), and k(a) \subseteq k(\kappa)(a) has dimension \le m over k(\kappa); hence a is algebraic over k. \square

=====================================================================
CLAIM 4 (Zariski's lemma). Let E be a field which is a finitely generated k-algebra. Then E is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

Proof. Write E = k[x_1,\dots,x_n] as a k-algebra. Since E is a field, k(x_1,\dots,x_n) \subseteq E and it contains k[x_1,\dots,x_n] = E, so E = k(x_1,\dots,x_n).

Apply (3f) to get algebraically independent t_1,\dots,t_r \in E such that E is algebraic over F := k(t_1,\dots,t_r). Set R := k[t_1,\dots,t_r]; algebraic independence means R is a polynomial ring, hence a domain, and since E is a field the inclusion R \hookrightarrow E extends to an inclusion of fields F = \mathrm{Frac}(R) \hookrightarrow E. Also E = F[x_1,\dots,x_n] (as F \subseteq E and x_i \in E), and each x_i is algebraic over F because E/F is algebraic; therefore E is a finite-dimensional F-vector space: by induction, F[a_1,\dots,a_m] is finite-dimensional over F whenever the a_i are algebraic over F, since adjoining one algebraic element of degree d yields a space spanned by 1,a,\dots,a^{d-1}. Let \ell := \dim_F E and let w_1,\dots,w_\ell be an F-basis of E.

Define the R-submodule M := \sum_{j=1}^{\ell} R w_j \subseteq E; it is a free R-module with basis the w_j (R-linear independence follows from F-linear independence).

We record three denominator facts. Since E = \sum_j F w_j:
\quad (D1) each x_i = \sum_j \lambda_{ij} w_j with \lambda_{ij} \in F; taking a common denominator b_1 \neq 0 in R for all \lambda_{ij}, we get x_i \in (1/b_1)M for all i;
\quad (D2) each w_j w_{j'} = \sum_m \mu_{jj'm} w_m with \mu_{jj'm} \in F; taking a common denominator b_2 \neq 0, we get M\cdot M \subseteq (1/b_2)M;
\quad (D3) 1 = \sum_j \nu_j w_j with \nu_j \in F; taking a common denominator b_3 \neq 0, we get 1 \in (1/b_3)M.
Put b := b_1 b_2 b_3 \in R \setminus \{0\} and g := b^2 \in R \setminus \{0\}. Then (1/b_\nu)M \subseteq (1/g)M for \nu = 1,2,3 (since g/b_\nu = b^2/b_\nu \in R), and M \subseteq (1/g)M (as m = g^{-1}(gm) with gm \in M). Consequently:
\quad x_i \in (1/g)M for all i,\quad 1 \in (1/g)M,\quad M\cdot M \subseteq (1/g)M.
Now define N := \sum_{m \ge 0} (1/g)^m M \subseteq E. Because (1/g)^m M \subseteq (1/g)^{m+1} M, N is an increasing union of R-submodules, hence an R-submodule, and in fact N = \sum_{j=1}^{\ell} R[1/g]\, w_j is a finitely generated module over the ring R[1/g] (viewed inside E; it is a genuine subring since R is a domain and g \neq 0). N is closed under multiplication: (1/g)^s M \cdot (1/g)^{s'} M \subseteq (1/g)^{s+s'}(1/g)M = (1/g)^{s+s'+1}M \subseteq N. And 1 \in (1/g)M \subseteq N. So N is a subring of E, and it contains R (as 1 \in N and N is an R-module) and 1/g (as 1 \in (1/g)M gives 1/g \in (1/g)^2 M \subseteq N). Thus N contains R[1/g].
Moreover N \subseteq E (clear: E is a ring containing (1/g) and M) and E \subseteq N, because E = k[x_1,\dots,x_n] is generated as a ring over k by the x_i, and k \subseteq R \subseteq N while each x_i \in N and N is a subring. Hence E = N, and therefore:
\quad (\dagger) E is a finitely generated module over the subring S := R[1/g] = k[t_1,\dots,t_r,1/g].
By (3e) applied to S \subseteq E, E is integral over S; by (3f)... rather, by (3e) directly: since S \subseteq E with E a field and E a finite S-module, (3e) says S is a field. If r \ge 1, this contradicts (3c). Hence r = 0.
With r = 0, the transcendence basis is empty, so E is algebraic over k. Each x_i is then algebraic over k, hence integral over k (a monic minimal polynomial), and as in (3f)'s parenthetical argument k[x_1,\dots,x_n] is a finitely generated k-module: inductively, if B' is a finite-dimensional k-vector space and a \in E is integral over B' (the same monic polynomial over k shows integrality over any larger base ring), then B'[a] is spanned over B' by 1,a,\dots,a^{d-1}. Thus E is finite-dimensional over k. \square

=====================================================================
CONCLUSION. Take E and \varphi as in Claim 2. Then E is a field and a finitely generated k-algebra, so by Claim 4 E is finite over k; \varphi: A \to E is a k-algebra homomorphism (composition of the k-algebra maps \iota and q); and \varphi(f) = q(\iota(f)) is a unit of the field E, hence nonzero. This is exactly the required conclusion. \square

(All steps were justified explicitly: injectivity of A \to A_f by coefficient comparison; existence of the maximal ideal by Zorn; Zariski's lemma by the transcendence-basis/denominator argument with the determinant trick, using only Euclid's argument for infinitely many irreducibles, primeness of irreducibles in k[t_1] and its polynomial extensions, and elementary integrality facts. No Noether normalization was invoked, so the defect identified in the earlier attempt does not arise.)
