Integrality/equidimensionality. Since Y is integral, M is integral: cover Y by affine opens Spec B_nu (B_nu domains); M is covered by Spec(B_nu[t]), which are integral, and these opens pairwise meet because Y is irreducible; M is reduced. Similarly U(f) is integral (opens Spec S'^{-1}B_nu[t]). Also Y_eta is integral: (Spec B_nu) x_k Spec K = Spec(S^{-1}(B_nu[t])) is the spectrum of a non-zero domain, and these opens cover Y_eta and pairwise meet. Finally Y_eta is smooth of pure dimension d over the field K (base change of the smooth k-scheme Y), and M and U(f) are smooth of pure dimension d+1 over k. All these schemes are therefore reduced, equidimensional and catenary, so for an integral closed subscheme T of such a scheme X one has codim_X(T) = dim X - dim T.

Conventions (standard Chow theory with integral coefficients).
(C1) Definition of divisor on a possibly non-normal integral scheme. If V is an integral scheme of finite type over a field, with normalization eps: V~ -> V (which exists and is finite, V being a variety over a field), and r in k(V)^x, then div_V(r) := eps_* div_{V~}(r), where div_{V~}(r) = sum_{x in (V~)^{(1)}} ord_x(r) . cl_{V~}(x), and ord_x is the normalized valuation of the DVR O_{V~,x} (V~ is normal and noetherian, so its codimension-1 local rings are DVRs; the sum is finite because r is a unit on a non-empty open subset of the noetherian scheme V~). This is the standard definition; it is used consistently on Y_eta, on M and on every U(f), and no normality of V is ever assumed.
(C2) Rat^n(V) is the subgroup of Z^n(V) generated by the cycles (iota_W)_* div_W(s) with W an integral closed subscheme of V of codimension n-1 and s in k(W)^x; if n = 0 there are no such W, so Rat^0(V) = 0. CH^n(V) := Z^n(V)/Rat^n(V). Every element of Rat^n(V) is a FINITE sum of such generators.
(C3) Pushforward of cycles along proper maps of finite type over a field: for T integral closed in X and f: X -> Y proper, f_*[T] := [k(T):k(f(T))] . [f(T)] if dim f(T) = dim T, and 0 otherwise; extended linearly. For a closed immersion the degree is 1 and f(T) is the image with reduced structure. Only closed immersions and finite maps are used below, so only this cycle-level operation is needed.
(C4) Restriction to an open: for an open immersion j: V' -> V and a cycle sum n_i[T_i], j^* sum n_i[T_i] := sum_{T_i cap V' != empty} n_i[T_i cap V']. Since V' is open, T_i cap V' is empty or integral of the same codimension, so this maps Z^n(V) -> Z^n(V'); it is the flat pullback of cycles along j.

Trivial cases. If n < 0 or n > d+1 then Z^n(M) = 0, so gamma = 0 and j_1^* gamma = 0; take f = 1. If n = 0: M is integral, so Z^0(M) = Z.[M] and CH^0(M) = Z.[M] by (C2). By Claim 2.3 below, i^*[M] = res_M[M] = [M_eta] = [Y_eta], which is the non-zero generator of Z^0(Y_eta) = CH^0(Y_eta) = Z.[Y_eta] (Y_eta is integral). Hence i^* gamma = 0 forces gamma = 0, and again f = 1 works. In the sequel we assume 1 <= n <= d+1.

=============================================================
1. GENERIC FIBRES
=============================================================

Claim 1.1. Let V be an integral k-scheme of finite type and q: V -> A^1 a morphism with q(xi_V) = eta. Then V_eta := V x_{A^1} Spec K is integral, its generic point is xi_V, k(V_eta) = k(V), and dim V_eta = dim V - 1.
Proof. Cover V by affine opens V_lam = Spec B_lam; every one contains xi_V. The composite R -> Gamma(V,O_V) -> B_lam -> k(V) has kernel the prime of R cut out by q(xi_V) = eta, namely (0); hence R injects into B_lam. Thus B_lam is a domain containing R, S contains no zero of B_lam, and (V_lam)_eta = Spec(S^{-1}B_lam) is the spectrum of a non-zero domain, i.e. an integral scheme; it contains xi_V (the prime (0) of B_lam is disjoint from S). The standard description of the spectrum of a localization says that (V_lam)_eta -> V_lam identifies |V_lam_eta| homeomorphically with the subspace {x in |V_lam| : q(x) = eta} of |V_lam|; gluing, |V_eta| is the subspace q^{-1}(eta) of |V|.
V_eta is reduced (covered by reduced opens) and irreducible: if V_eta = F_1 union F_2 with F_nu closed, then xi_V lies in one of them, say F_1; F_1 = C cap V_eta with C closed in V, and xi_V in C forces C = V, hence F_1 = V_eta. So V_eta is integral. Its generic point is xi_V: for any x in V_eta, the closure of {x} in V contains xi_V, so the closure of {x} in the subspace V_eta = cl_V(x) cap q^{-1}(eta) contains xi_V. Therefore k(V_eta) = O_{V_eta,xi_V} = O_{V,xi_V} = k(V) (localizing at S does not change the local ring at a prime disjoint from S). Finally, since V_eta is integral of finite type over the field K, dim V_eta = trdeg_K k(V_eta) = trdeg_K k(V) = trdeg_k k(V) - trdeg_k K = dim V - 1, using trdeg_k k(V) = dim V (V integral, finitely generated over k) and trdeg_k K = 1 (R injects into k(V), proved above). QED

Claim 1.2. Let V be an integral closed subscheme of M of codimension m. Exactly one of the following holds.
(a) V is contained in p^{-1}(s) for a closed point s of A^1; then V x_M Y_eta = empty.
(b) V dominates A^1; then V_eta := V x_M Y_eta is integral of codimension m in Y_eta with k(V_eta) = k(V), |V_eta| = |V| cap p^{-1}(eta) with the subspace topology, and V is the closure of V_eta in M.
Proof. The restriction p|_V: V -> A^1 is proper: V is closed in Y x_k A^1 and the projection Y x_k A^1 -> A^1 is projective (base change of Y -> Spec k, which is projective). Hence p(V) is closed in A^1, and it is irreducible since V is. So p(V) is A^1 or a single closed point ({eta} is not closed). In case (a) the fibre product is empty because Spec K -> A^1 meets no closed point. Otherwise p(V) = A^1; since V and A^1 are integral, q(xi_V) is the generic point of p(V), i.e. eta, so Claim 1.1 applies to (V, p|_V) (and V x_M Y_eta = V x_{A^1}

Spec K). Hence V_eta is integral, k(V_eta)=k(V), dim V_eta=dim V-1. Since V_eta is closed in Y_eta and dim Y_eta=d, codim_{Y_eta}(V_eta)=d-(dim V-1). But dim V=d+1-m, so this equals m. The underlying space of V_eta is |V| cap p^{-1}(eta); because it contains xi_V, V is the closure of V_eta in M. Exactly one of (a) and (b) holds because p(V) is a closed irreducible subset of A^1, hence either a closed point or all of A^1. QED

Claim 1.3. Define the elementary generic-fibre restriction res_M on integral codimension-n cycles by res_M[V]=[V_eta] if V dominates A^1 and res_M[V]=0 if V is contained in a closed fibre, and extend linearly to Z^n(M). If W in Z^n(M) satisfies res_M(W)=0, then there exists a nonzero g in R such that the restriction of W to U(g) is the zero cycle.
Proof. Write W=sum n_i [V_i] with distinct integral components V_i. The dominating V_i have distinct generic fibres: if V_i dominates, Claim 1.2 says V_i is the closure of (V_i)_eta, so equality of generic fibres implies equality of V_i. Thus res_M(W)=0 forces all coefficients of dominating components to vanish after combining; hence every V_i lies in a closed fibre. The images p(V_i) are finitely many closed points of A^1. For each such point s choose the monic irreducible polynomial h_s in R defining s, and let g be the product of these h_s, or g=1 if there are none. Then D(g) contains no p(V_i), so V_i cap U(g)=empty for every i, and W|_{U(g)}=0. QED

=============================================================
2. SPREADING OUT RATIONAL EQUIVALENCE AND FLAT PULLBACK
=============================================================

Claim 2.1. Let W be an integral closed subscheme of Y_eta of codimension n-1 and let r in k(W)^x. Let A be the closure of W in M with reduced structure, and let i_A:A->M and i_W:W->Y_eta be the closed immersions. Then A is integral of codimension n-1 in M, dominates A^1, A_eta=W as reduced schemes, k(A)=k(W), and
res_M((i_A)_* div_A(r)) = (i_W)_* div_W(r).
Proof. The underlying space of A_eta is |A| cap p^{-1}(eta), which is the closure of |W| in the subspace Y_eta; since W is closed in Y_eta this is |W|. By Claim 1.1 applied to A, A_eta is integral and reduced, so A_eta=W as reduced schemes. Also dim A=dim W+1, hence codim_M A = codim_{Y_eta} W = n-1, and k(A)=k(A_eta)=k(W).

Let nu:N->A be the normalization. Then N is normal integral and finite over A. Put V=N_eta and let f:N->M be the composite. Since integral closure commutes with localization, V is the normalization of W, and f_eta:V->Y_eta is the composite. The function r is an element of k(N)^x. By (C1), div_A(r)=nu_* div_N(r), so (i_A)_*div_A(r)=f_*div_N(r). Similarly div_W(r)=(V->W)_*div_V(r), hence (i_W)_*div_W(r)=f_eta_*div_V(r). It remains to prove res_M(f_*div_N(r))=f_eta_*div_V(r).

Write div_N(r)=sum_{x in N^{(1)}} a_x [Z_x], where Z_x is the closure of x and a_x=ord_x(r). If p(x) is a closed point of A^1, then the image p(Z_x) is the closure of {p(x)}, hence a closed point, so Z_x lies in a closed fibre; then f_*[Z_x] is supported in a closed fibre and its res_M is zero. Such x are not points of V. If p(x)=eta, then Z_x dominates A^1. By Claim 1.1 applied to Z_x, (Z_x)_eta is integral of codimension 1 in V, its generic point is x, and k((Z_x)_eta)=k(Z_x). The image f(Z_x) also dominates A^1, and by Claim 1.1 applied to f(Z_x) its generic fibre f(Z_x)_eta is integral with function field k(f(Z_x)). Moreover f_eta((Z_x)_eta)=f(Z_x)_eta by base change and lying over for the finite map f. Since f is finite, f_*[Z_x]=[k(Z_x):k(f(Z_x))] [f(Z_x)], and applying res_M gives the same degree times [f(Z_x)_eta]. On the other hand, f_eta_*[(Z_x)_eta]=[k((Z_x)_eta):k(f(Z_x)_eta)] [f(Z_x)_eta]. The two field degrees are equal by the preceding identifications. Finally, because x lies over eta, every nonzero element of S is a unit in O_{N,x}; hence O_{N,x}=S^{-1}O_{N,x}=O_{V,x}, so the valuation a_x=ord_x(r) is the same when computed in N or in V. The points x of N^{(1)} lying over eta are exactly the points of V^{(1)}: for such x, codim_N(x)=codim_V(x) by the dimension formula in Claim 1.1, and every codimension-one point of V is such an x. Summing over x gives the desired equality. QED

Claim 2.2. Let A be as in Claim 2.1 and let 0 != g in R. Put U=U(g), A_U=A x_M U. Then the restriction of (i_A)_*div_A(r) to U is (i_{A_U})_*div_{A_U}(r), and is zero if A_U is empty.
Proof. For a closed immersion and an open immersion the obvious square is cartesian, and on cycles restriction commutes with pushforward: j^* (i_A)_* = (i_{A_U})_* j_A^*. It remains to check divisors. Let nu:N->A be the normalization and N_U=N x_A A_U. Then N_U is the normalization of A_U. The codimension-one points of N_U are precisely the codimension-one points of N contained in N_U; for such a point the local ring is unchanged, and the closure in A_U is the intersection with A_U of the closure in A. Therefore j_A^*div_N(r)=div_{N_U}(r). Pushing forward by nu gives the claim. QED

Claim 2.3. For every cycle W in Z^n(M), the flat pullback i^*W equals res_M(W).
Proof. It suffices to check an integral closed subscheme V of codimension n. If V is contained in a closed fibre, then V x_M Y_eta is empty, and the flat pullback of [V] is zero, equal to res_M[V]. If V dominates A^1, then by Claim 1.2 V_eta is integral of codimension n in Y_eta. The flat pullback formula for a flat morphism sends [V] to the sum over generic points x of V x_M Y_eta of length_{O_{V x_M Y_eta,x}} [closure of x]. Here there is only one generic point, xi_V, and its local ring is the field k(V_eta), so the length is 1. Thus i^*[V]=[V_eta]=res_M[V]. QED

In particular, for gamma in CH^n(M), the hypothesis i^*gamma=0 means that for any cycle representative Z of gamma the cycle res_M(Z) is rationally equivalent to zero on Y_eta.

=============================================================
3. END OF PROOF
=============================================================

Choose a cycle representative Z in Z^n(M) of gamma. Since i^*gamma=0, Claim 2.3 gives res_M(Z)=0 in CH^n(Y_eta). Hence, by the definition of rational equivalence, there are finitely many integral closed subschemes W_j of Y_eta of codimension n-1 and rational functions r_j in k(W_j)^x such that
res_M(Z)=sum_j (i_{W_j})_* div_{W_j}(r_j).
For each j let A_j be the closure of W_j in M with reduced structure, and define
Gamma_j=(i_{A_j})_* div_{A_j}(r_j) in Z^n(M).
By Claim 2.2, res_M(Gamma_j)=(i_{W_j})_* div_{W_j}(r_j). Therefore
res_M(Z-sum_j Gamma_j)=0.
Claim 1.3 gives a nonzero g in R such that (Z-sum_j Gamma_j)|_{U(g)}=0 as a cycle. Thus
Z|_{U(g)}=sum_j Gamma_j|_{U(g)}.
By Claim 2.2, each Gamma_j|_{U(g)} is (i_{A_{j,g}})_* div_{A_{j,g}}(r_j), where A_{j,g}=A_j x_M U(g). If A_{j,g} is nonempty it is an integral closed subscheme of U(g) of codimension n-1, so this cycle is rationally equivalent to zero on U(g); if it is empty the cycle is zero. Hence Z|_{U(g)} is rationally equivalent to zero on U(g). Passing to Chow classes, j_g^*gamma=0 in CH^n(U(g)). Setting f=g gives the required nonzero polynomial. QED"
}

statement: Let $Y$ be a smooth quasi-projective variety over a field $k$, let $M=Y\times_k\mathbb{A}^1_k$, let $\mathrm{pr}:M\to Y$ be the projection and let $s:Y\to M$ be the zero section of the trivial line bundle, a regular embedding of codimension $1$. Then for every $n\ge 0$ and every $\gamma\in\mathrm{CH}^n(Y)$ with integral coefficients, the refined Gysin pullback satisfies $s^{!}(\mathrm{pr}^{*}\gamma)=\gamma$ in $\mathrm{CH}^n(Y)$.
proof:
Let D = s(Y) = Y ×_k {0} ⊂ M = Y ×_k A^1_k. Write t for the standard coordinate on A^1_k. On an affine open Spec A ⊂ Y we have M = Spec A[t] and D = V(t). Since A[t]/(t) ≅ A and multiplication by t is injective, (t) is locally generated by a non-zero divisor; hence D is an effective Cartier divisor. The regular embedding s is the inclusion i:D ↪ M followed by the isomorphism s:D → Y.

For a Cartier divisor D, the refined Gysin pullback along the inclusion i:D ↪ M is the intersection product with D. In the special case needed here, if W ⊂ M is an integral closed subscheme not contained in D and meeting D properly, then i^![W] = D·[W] = Σ_{ξ ∈ (W∩D)^(0)} length_{O_{W,ξ}}(O_{W,ξ}/(t)) [i^{-1}(ξ)]. This is the usual defining computation of the refined Gysin map for a Cartier divisor in the proper-intersection case.

Every element of CH^n(Y) is represented by a finite integral cycle Σ m_i[V_i] with V_i integral closed subschemes of codimension n. Since pr^* and s^! are homomorphisms, it is enough to prove the formula for γ = [V] for one such V.

Because pr is flat, pr^*[V] = [W] where W = V ×_k A^1_k. The subscheme W is integral and has codimension n in M. Moreover W is not contained in D, and W∩D = (V ×_k A^1_k) ∩ (Y ×_k {0}) = V ×_k {0}. The intersection is proper: locally on an affine open U = Spec A of V, W_U = Spec A[t] and (W∩D)_U = Spec A[t]/(t) = Spec A; the element t is a non-zero divisor, so the intersection has codimension 1 in W. Thus there is a single generic point ξ of W∩D, lying over the generic point η of V.

At this generic point, O_{W,ξ} ≅ κ(V)[t]_{(t)}. The local equation of D is t, so the intersection multiplicity is length_{O_{W,ξ}}(O_{W,ξ}/(t)) = length_{κ(V)[t]_{(t)}}(κ(V)) = 1, because κ(V)[t]_{(t)} is a discrete valuation ring with maximal ideal (t), and the quotient by (t) is its residue field. Therefore s^!pr^*[V] = i^![W] = [V ×_k {0}] = [V] under the identification D ≅ Y.

By additivity, for a general cycle representative Z = Σ m_i[V_i] of γ we get s^!pr^*[Z] = Σ m_i s^!pr^*[V_i] = Σ m_i[V_i] = [Z] = γ. If Z' is another cycle representative of the same class, then pr^*Z and pr^*Z' represent the same class in CH^n(M), and s^! is well-defined on Chow groups; hence the same equality holds for the class γ. Thus s^!(pr^*γ) = γ for all γ ∈ CH^n(Y).

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d and C/k a smooth integral curve, and let p_{12}, p_{23}, p_{13}\colon X\times_k X\times_k X\times_k C \to X\times_k X\times_k C be induced by (x_1,x_2,x_3,s) \mapsto (x_1,x_2,s), (x_2,x_3,s), (x_1,x_3,s). If \gamma \in \mathrm{CH}^{d}(X\times_k X\times_k C) has a cycle representative whose support is contained in (X\times_k X)\times_k T for a finite set T of closed points of C, then p_{13*}(p_{12}^{*}\gamma \cdot p_{23}^{*}\gamma) = 0 in \mathrm{CH}^{d}(X\times_k X\times_k C).
proof:
PROOF OF lemma_68.

=== Notation ===
Write Y := X \times_k X \times_k C and Z := X \times_k X \times_k X \times_k C, and let p_{12},p_{23},p_{13}:Z\to Y be the maps of the statement, induced by (x_1,x_2,x_3,s)\mapsto(x_1,x_2,s), (x_2,x_3,s), (x_1,x_3,s). Write T=\{t_1,\dots,t_m\}; each t_i is a closed point of C and \kappa(t_i) is its residue field. By a "smooth integral curve over k" we understand an integral k-scheme which is separated, of finite type and smooth of pure relative dimension 1; in particular C is smooth, separated and of finite type over k, and C is a regular noetherian 1-dimensional scheme.

X is smooth projective of pure dimension d over k, hence so are X^2 (dimension 2d) and X^3 (dimension 3d). Therefore Y is smooth of pure dimension 2d+1 over k and Z is smooth of pure dimension 3d+1 over k; in particular
   CH^d(Y)=CH_{d+1}(Y),  CH^d(Z)=CH_{2d+1}(Z),  CH^{2d}(Z)=CH_{d+1}(Z),
and CH(Y), CH(Z) carry their usual intersection products, defined through the diagonal regular embeddings \Delta_{Y/k},\Delta_{Z/k}.

=== Part 0. Background facts from intersection theory ===
We record the standard results we use, with the precise hypotheses we verify for each application. All are from Fulton, *Intersection Theory*.

(BF1) *Projection formula and self-intersection formula for a codimension-1 regular embedding.* Let W be a variety smooth over a field, let j:V\hookrightarrow W be a closed immersion which is a regular embedding of pure codimension 1 with normal bundle N_{V/W}, and suppose V is smooth over a field (not necessarily the same field as W, so that CH(V) has its own intersection product, defined via the diagonal V\to V\times V over *that* field). Then the refined Gysin homomorphism j^!:\mathrm{CH}(W)\to\mathrm{CH}(V) (codimension-preserving, [Ful, \S6.1, \S6.2]) satisfies, for all \xi,\eta\in\mathrm{CH}(V),
   (j_*\xi)\cdot(j_*\eta) \;=\; j_*\big(\xi\cdot j^!j_*\eta\big) \;=\; j_*\big(\xi\cdot (c_1(N_{V/W})\cap\eta)\big),
where the first equality is the projection formula [Ful, Thm. 6.2(a)] applied to the cartesian square V\to V over W\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}W, and the second is the self-intersection formula j^!j_*\eta=c_1(N_{V/W})\cap\eta [Ful, \S6.2--6.3; the proof of both statements runs through the deformation to the normal cone and uses no base-field hypothesis on V or W beyond the existence of the intersection products that appear]. Consequently: if c_1(N_{V/W})=0 in \mathrm{CH}^1(V) (e.g. if N_{V/W} is a trivial line bundle), then (j_*\xi)\cdot(j_*\eta)=0 in CH(W) for all \xi,\eta.

(BF2) *Flat base change for Chow groups.* For a cartesian square
  V' --j'--> V
  |g'        |g
  W' --j--> W
with g flat and j a closed immersion, j^*g_* = g'_*j'^* on Chow groups ([Ful, Prop. 1.7]).

(BF3) *Ideal sheaves under flat base change of a closed immersion.* In the cartesian square of (BF2), if g is defined by the ideal sheaf I on W and j is flat, then the ideal sheaf I' of j' satisfies I'/I'^2 \cong j'^*(I/I^2) (Tor-independence of the square gives the standard isomorphism; equivalently, an effective Cartier divisor pulls back to an effective Cartier divisor whose conormal sheaf is the pullback of the conormal sheaf).

(BF4) *Chern classes.* A trivial line bundle has vanishing first Chern class (c_1(O)=0, since O=O(\mathrm{div}(1)) and principal Cartier divisors act trivially, [Ful, Prop. 2.3]); the cap product c_1(L)\cap - is additive in the class c_1(L), hence is the zero operation when c_1(L)=0.

(BF5) *Proper pushforward and flat pullback preserve dimension grading* ([Ful, 1.4, 1.7]); in particular flat pullback preserves codimension, closed immersions preserve dimension, and proper pushforward preserves dimension.

=== Part 1. The case d=0 ===
If d=0 then X is finite \'etale over k, X\times_kX is 0-dimensional, and Y=X\times_kX\times_kC is a finite disjoint union of integral curves, so \dim Y=1 and CH^0(Y)=CH_1(Y) is the free abelian group on the integral 1-dimensional closed subschemes of Y. A representative of \gamma supported on (X\times X)\times T is a 1-cycle supported on a 0-dimensional scheme, hence is the empty cycle: \gamma=0. Then p_{13*}(p_{12}^*\gamma\cdot p_{23}^*\gamma)=0. Henceforth assume d\ge 1.

=== Part 2. Decomposition of \gamma along the fibers ===
For each i let j_i:X^2_{t_i}:=X\times_kX\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t_i)\longrightarrow Y be the closed immersion (base change of \mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t_i)\hookrightarrow C). Let F:=(X\times_kX)\times_k T\hookrightarrow Y, where T carries the reduced structure, so F=\coprod_{i=1}^{m}X^2_{t_i}.

By hypothesis \gamma has a cycle representative Z=\sum_\nu n_\nu Z_\nu whose support lies in (X\times_kX)\times_kT. Each Z_\nu is an integral closed subscheme of Y of dimension (2d+1)-d=d+1 contained in the reduced closed subscheme F, hence Z_\nu is an integral closed subscheme of F with the same function field, so the same formal sum defines a cycle Z' on F with i_*Z'=Z as cycles on Y, where i:F\hookrightarrow Y is the closed immersion (proper pushforward, BF5). Thus \gamma=i_*[Z']. Since Chow groups of a disjoint union split as a direct sum, [Z']=\sum_i[\gamma_i'] with \gamma_i' a (d+1)-dimensional cycle on X^2_{t_i}. Now X is smooth of pure dimension d over k, so X^2_{t_i}\cong X^2_{\kappa(t_i)} is smooth projective of pure dimension 2d over the field \kappa(t_i); hence dimension-(d+1) cycles on X^2_{t_i} are exactly codimension-(2d-(d+1))=codimension-(d-1) cycles. Setting \gamma_i:=[\gamma_i']\in CH^{d-1}(X^2_{t_i}) we obtain
   \gamma=\sum_{i=1}^{m} j_{i*}\gamma_i \quad\text{in } CH^d(Y),
since j_i=i\circ(\text{component inclusion}) and j_{i*}\gamma_i=i_*[\gamma_i'].

=== Part 3. Bilinearity ===
p_{12} and p_{23} are flat of relative dimension d (base changes of the projection X^3\to X^2, which is smooth of relative dimension d), so p_{12}^*,p_{23}^*:CH^d(Y)\to CH^d(Z) are group homomorphisms (BF5), and p_{13} is proper (base change of the proper projection X^3\to X^2), so p_{13*}:CH_{d+1}(Z)\to CH_{d+1}(Y) is a group homomorphism. Since the intersection product on CH(Z) is bilinear,
   p_{13*}\big(p_{12}^*\gamma\cdot p_{23}^*\gamma\big)=\sum_{i,l=1}^{m} p_{13*}\Big(\big(p_{12}^*j_{i*}\gamma_i\big)\cdot\big(p_{23}^*j_{l*}\gamma_l\big)\Big) \quad\text{in } CH^d(Y),
each summand lying in CH^{2d}(Z)=CH_{d+1}(Z) before the pushforward.

=== Part 4. The off-diagonal terms i\neq l vanish (lemma_47) ===
Take S:=C in lemma_47: C is smooth, separated and of finite type over k, so its hypotheses on S are satisfied, and with S=C the schemes Y=X\times_kX\times_kS, Z=X\times_kX\times_kX\times_kS and the maps p_{12},p_{23},p_{13} of lemma_47 are exactly ours. For i\neq l put T_0:=\{t_i\}, T_1:=\{t_l\}: these are closed subsets of C (closed points of a finite type scheme over a field are closed) and they are disjoint because the t_i are distinct. The class U:=j_{i*}\gamma_i\in CH^d(Y) is represented by the cycle j_{i*}\gamma_i', whose support is contained in X^2_{t_i}=(X\times_kX)\times_kT_0, and V:=j_{l*}\gamma_l\in CH^d(Y) is represented by a cycle supported in (X\times_kX)\times_kT_1. Lemma 47 therefore gives
   p_{13*}\Big(\big(p_{12}^*j_{i*}\gamma_i\big)\cdot\big(p_{23}^*j_{l*}\gamma_l\big)\Big)=0 \qquad (i\neq l).

=== Part 5. The diagonal terms i=l vanish ===
Fix i and write t:=t_i, j:=j_i, \gamma_i\in CH^{d-1}(X^2_t). Let
   D:=X^3_t:=X\times_kX\times_kX\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t),
let k:D\to Z be the closed immersion, and let pr_{12},pr_{23}:D\to X^2_t be the projections (x_1,x_2,x_3)\mapsto(x_1,x_2), (x_2,x_3).

5.1 (Rewriting the two factors.) The square
   D --pr_{12}--> X^2_t
   k|             |j
   Z --p_{12}-->  Y
is cartesian: indeed X^2_t\times_Y Z = (X^2\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t))\times_{(X^2\times_kC)}(X^3\times_kC) = X^3\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t)=D, and similarly for p_{23}. Since p_{12} and p_{23} are flat, (BF2) yields
   p_{12}^*j_*\gamma_i = k_*pr_{12}^*\gamma_i, \qquad p_{23}^*j_*\gamma_i = k_*pr_{23}^*\gamma_i,
both classes in CH^d(Z) (flat pullback preserves the codimension index: pr_{12},pr_{23} are smooth of relative dimension d over \kappa(t), so pr_{12}^*\gamma_i,pr_{23}^*\gamma_i\in CH^{d-1}(D) and k_* raises codimension by 1 because k is a codimension-1 closed immersion; check: D has pure dimension 3d over the field \kappa(t), so CH^{d-1}(D)=CH_{3d-(d-1)}(D)=CH_{2d+1}(D) and CH^d(Z)=CH_{2d+1}(Z) — consistent with dimension-preserving pushforward).
Set a:=pr_{12}^*\gamma_i and b:=pr_{23}^*\gamma_i.

5.2 (k is a regular embedding of pure codimension 1 with trivial normal bundle.) Since C is regular of dimension 1 and t is a closed point, the ideal sheaf I_t of t in C is invertible: \{t\}\hookrightarrow C is an effective Cartier divisor, i.e. a regular embedding of pure codimension 1. The projection \pi:Z=X^3\times_kC\to C is flat, being the base change of X^3\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k, which is flat because X^3 is smooth over k. Hence D=\pi^{-1}(t)\to Z is the flat base change of an effective Cartier divisor, so by (BF3) it is an effective Cartier divisor, i.e. a regular embedding of pure codimension 1, and its ideal sheaf I_D satisfies
   I_D/I_D^2 \;\cong\; \mathrm{pr}_2^*(I_t/I_t^2)
where \mathrm{pr}_2:D\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t) is the structural morphism. Now I_t/I_t^2 is the conormal space of t in the regular 1-dimensional local scheme (C,t): it is the maximal ideal m_t/m_t^2 of the discrete valuation ring O_{C,t}, a vector space of dimension 1 over \kappa(t)=O_{C,t}/m_t; equivalently, I_t/I_t^2 is a 1-dimensional \kappa(t)-vector space. Choosing a \kappa(t)-basis gives I_t/I_t^2\cong\kappa(t), hence I_D/I_D^2\cong O_D and therefore the normal bundle N_{D/Z}:=(I_D/I_D^2)^\vee\cong O_D is a trivial line bundle. By (BF4), c_1(N_{D/Z})=0 in CH^1(D).

5.3 (D is smooth over the field \kappa(t).) D=X^3\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t) is the base change of the smooth k-scheme X^3 along \mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(t)\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k; smoothness is stable under arbitrary base change, so D is smooth of dimension 3d over the FIELD \kappa(t). In particular D is of finite type over a field, its Chow ring is defined via the diagonal D\to D\times_{\kappa(t)}D (a regular embedding because D is smooth over \kappa(t)), and all products of classes on D below are taken with respect to this \kappa(t)-structure. We stress that we never use that \kappa(t)/k is separable, nor that D is smooth over k (which may fail); the only properties of \kappa(t) used are that it is a field and that I_t/I_t^2 is 1-dimensional over it.

5.4 (Vanishing of the product.) Z is smooth of dimension 3d+1 over the field k, k:D\hookrightarrow Z is a regular embedding of pure codimension 1 with N_{D/Z} trivial, and a,b\in CH^{d-1}(D) with D smooth over the field \kappa(t). Applying (BF1) with W=Z, V=D, j=k, \xi=a, \eta=b, and using c_1(N_{D/Z})\cap b=0 by 5.2 and (BF4), we get in CH^{2d}(Z):
   \big(p_{12}^*j_*\gamma_i\big)\cdot\big(p_{23}^*j_*\gamma_i\big) = (k_*a)\cdot(k_*b) = k_*\big(a\cdot(k^!k_*b)\big) = k_*\big(a\cdot 0\big)=0 .
(Bookkeeping: a\in CH^{d-1}(D), k^!k_*b\in CH^{d}(D), so a\cdot k^!k_*b\in CH^{2d-1}(D) and k_* lands in CH^{2d}(Z), as required.)
Pushing forward by p_{13} gives
   p_{13*}\Big(\big(p_{12}^*j_{i*}\gamma_i\big)\cdot\big(p_{23}^*j_{i*}\gamma_i\big)\Big)=0 .

=== Part 6. Conclusion ===
Every summand of the expansion in Part 3 is zero: for i\neq l by Part 4 (lemma_47), for i=l by Part 5. Hence
   p_{13*}\big(p_{12}^*\gamma\cdot p_{23}^*\gamma\big)=0 \quad\text{in } CH^d(X\times_kX\times_kC),
which is the claim. \blacksquare

(Remarks on the proof's dependencies: the only lemma cited is lemma_47, applied with S=C; lemma_51 is deliberately not used, since its hypothesis that both the ambient and the divisor be smooth over the *same* base field k need not hold for D=X^3_t when \kappa(t)/k is inseparable — e.g. C=\mathbb P^1_k with k imperfect and t defined by x^p-a. The diagonal terms are instead handled by the self-intersection formula (BF1), which requires no separability. No pushforward along a non-proper morphism is used anywhere: the decomposition in Part 2 uses only the proper pushforward along the closed immersion F\hookrightarrow Y, and no claim about products of disjointly supported classes is needed, since the cross terms are disposed of by lemma_47.)

statement: Let $X/k$ be smooth projective of dimension $d$, and let $p_1,p_2:X\times X\to X$ be the projections. For a $d$-cycle $Z=\sum_i n_i Z_i$ on $X\times X$ let $\mathrm{lev}(Z)=\max_i(\dim p_1(Z_i)+\dim p_2(Z_i)-d)$, $\mathrm{lev}(0)=-1$, and for $\gamma\in\mathrm{CH}^d(X\times X)$ let $\ell(\gamma)$ be the minimum of $\mathrm{lev}(Z)$ over cycle representatives $Z$ of $\gamma$. Then $\ell(\gamma)=-1$ if and only if $\gamma=0$.
proof: Proof. The variety X x X has dimension 2d, so a cycle representing an element of CH^d(X x X) is a d-dimensional cycle Z = sum_i n_i Z_i, where each Z_i is a closed integral d-dimensional subvariety of X x X and each coefficient n_i is nonzero. For any such component, dim p_1(Z_i) <= d and dim p_2(Z_i) <= d, so lev(Z) always lies in the finite set {-1,0,...,d}; hence the minimum defining ell is attained. We first show that lev(Z) = -1 if and only if Z is the zero cycle. If Z = 0, this is the definition of lev(0). Conversely, assume Z is not the zero cycle. Then there is an index i with n_i != 0. Put A_i = p_1(Z_i) and B_i = p_2(Z_i). The projections p_1 and p_2 are proper because X is projective, so A_i and B_i are closed irreducible subvarieties of X. For every point z of Z_i, the pair (p_1(z), p_2(z)) is exactly z as a point of X x X; hence Z_i is contained in A_i x B_i. Therefore d = dim Z_i <= dim(A_i x B_i) = dim A_i + dim B_i, where the last equality is the standard dimension formula for the product of irreducible varieties over k. Thus dim p_1(Z_i) + dim p_2(Z_i) - d >= 0, and consequently lev(Z) = max_j(dim p_1(Z_j) + dim p_2(Z_j) - d) >= 0. This proves the claim. Now let gamma be in CH^d(X x X). If gamma = 0, the zero cycle is a representative of gamma, and by the claim every representative has lev at least -1 while the zero representative has lev -1; hence ell(gamma) = -1. Conversely, if ell(gamma) = -1, then by the definition of ell as a minimum there is a cycle representative Z of gamma with lev(Z) = -1. By the claim, Z must be the zero cycle, so gamma is the class of the zero cycle, namely gamma = 0. Therefore ell(gamma) = -1 if and only if gamma = 0.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, and let p_1, p_2: X x X -> X be the projections. For a d-cycle Z = \sum_i n_i Z_i on X x X let lev(Z) = \max_i (\dim p_1(Z_i) + \dim p_2(Z_i) - d), lev(0) = -1, and for \gamma \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X x X) let \ell(\gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of \gamma. proof:
We prove the biconditional in two directions, using a preliminary dimension estimate that replaces the erroneous fiber-dimension argument from the previous attempt.

**Preliminary fact.** Let V be an integral closed subvariety of X \times_k X of dimension d. Then
  d \leq \dim p_1(V) + \dim p_2(V) \leq 2d.

*Proof of preliminary fact.*
(a) Since X is projective over k, X \times_k X is projective over k. The projection p_1: X \times_k X \to X is proper: it is the base change of the proper morphism X \to \mathrm{Spec}\,k by the morphism X \to \mathrm{Spec}\,k (and similarly for p_2). Hence p_1(V) and p_2(V) are closed subsets of X.
(b) The restriction p_1|_V: V \to p_1(V) is surjective by definition of the image. Since V is integral, its image p_1(V) under this surjective morphism is an integral closed subvariety of X (the continuous image of an irreducible set is irreducible, and the function field k(p_1(V)) embeds into k(V) via (p_1|_V)^\#, so k(p_1(V)) is a field, meaning p_1(V) is reduced; together with irreducibility this gives integrality). Similarly p_2(V) is an integral closed subvariety of X.
(c) Set a := \dim p_1(V) and b := \dim p_2(V). Since p_1(V) \subseteq X and X has dimension d, we have a \leq d. Similarly b \leq d.
(d) Set-theoretically, V \subseteq p_1(V) \times_k p_2(V): for any point (x,y) \in V, we have x = p_1(x,y) \in p_1(V) and y = p_2(x,y) \in p_2(V), so (x,y) \in p_1(V) \times_k p_2(V).
(e) The product p_1(V) \times_k p_2(V) is a closed subvariety of X \times_k X (product of two closed subvarieties of X), and its dimension is \dim p_1(V) + \dim p_2(V) = a + b (standard fact: for varieties over a field, \dim(V' \times_k W') = \dim V' + \dim W', since the transcendence degree of the function field of the product is the sum of the transcendence degrees).
(f) Since V is closed in X \times_k X and V \subseteq p_1(V) \times_k p_2(V), the variety V is a closed subvariety of p_1(V) \times_k p_2(V). As V is integral of dimension d, we have d = \dim V \leq \dim(p_1(V) \times_k p_2(V)) = a + b.
(g) Combining (c) and (f): d \leq a + b \leq d + d = 2d. This proves the preliminary fact. \square

**Corollary (bounds on lev).** For any non-zero d-cycle Z = \sum_i n_i Z_i on X \times_k X (each Z_i an integral d-dimensional closed subvariety), we have 0 \leq \mathrm{lev}(Z) \leq d. Also \mathrm{lev}(0) = -1 by definition.

*Proof.* For each i, applying the preliminary fact to V = Z_i gives d \leq \dim p_1(Z_i) + \dim p_2(Z_i) \leq 2d, hence 0 \leq \dim p_1(Z_i) + \dim p_2(Z_i) - d \leq d. Taking the maximum over i yields 0 \leq \mathrm{lev}(Z) \leq d. For Z = 0 (the empty cycle), \mathrm{lev}(0) = -1 by definition. \square

**Direction (\Rightarrow): \ell(\gamma) = d implies every representative has a full-dimensional component.**

Assume \ell(\gamma) = d. Let Z = \sum_i n_i Z_i be any d-cycle representative of \gamma (so [Z] = \gamma in \mathrm{CH}^d(X \times_k X)).

*Step A: Z \neq 0.* Suppose for contradiction that Z = 0. Then \gamma = [0] = 0 in \mathrm{CH}^d(X \times_k X). Since the zero cycle 0 is a d-cycle representative of \gamma = 0, we have \ell(\gamma) \leq \mathrm{lev}(0) = -1 by the definition of \ell as the minimum over all representatives. But \ell(\gamma) = d \geq 0 (since d is the dimension of X and d \geq 0; if d = 0 then X is a finite set of points and X \times X is zero-dimensional, so d = 0 and \ell(\gamma) = 0, while \mathrm{lev}(0) = -1 < 0, giving the same contradiction). In all cases \ell(\gamma) \leq -1 contradicts \ell(\gamma) = d. Hence Z \neq 0.

*Step B: \mathrm{lev}(Z) = d.* By definition, \ell(\gamma) = \min \{\mathrm{lev}(Z') : Z' \text{ is a d-cycle representative of } \gamma\}. Since \ell(\gamma) = d, we have \mathrm{lev}(Z) \geq d for every representative Z of \gamma. In particular, \mathrm{lev}(Z) \geq d. By the corollary (Z \neq 0), \mathrm{lev}(Z) \leq d. Therefore \mathrm{lev}(Z) = d.

*Step C: Existence of a full-dimensional component.* We have
  \mathrm{lev}(Z) = \max_i (\dim p_1(Z_i) + \dim p_2(Z_i) - d) = d.
By the definition of the maximum (taken over a finite non-empty set of indices, since Z \neq 0), there exists an index j such that
  \dim p_1(Z_j) + \dim p_2(Z_j) - d = d,
i.e., \dim p_1(Z_j) + \dim p_2(Z_j) = 2d.
Now p_1(Z_j) is a closed subset of X, so \dim p_1(Z_j) \leq d. Similarly \dim p_2(Z_j) \leq d. Since the sum of two integers each at most d equals 2d, both must equal d:
  \dim p_1(Z_j) = d \quad \text{and} \quad \dim p_2(Z_j) = d.
Thus Z has an integral component Z_j with \dim p_1(Z_j) = \dim p_2(Z_j) = d. Since Z was an arbitrary representative of \gamma, every d-cycle representative of \gamma has such a component. \square

**Direction (\Leftarrow): Every representative has a full-dimensional component implies \ell(\gamma) = d.**

Assume that every d-cycle representative of \gamma has an integral component Z_i with \dim p_1(Z_i) = \dim p_2(Z_i) = d.

*Step A: \gamma \neq 0.* The zero cycle 0 is a d-cycle on X \times_k X (the empty formal sum of integral d-dimensional subvarieties) and represents the zero class in \mathrm{CH}^d(X \times_k X). If \gamma = 0, then the zero cycle 0 is a d-cycle representative of \gamma. The hypothesis requires that 0 have an integral component Z_i with \dim p_1(Z_i) = \dim p_2(Z_i) = d. But the zero cycle has no integral components (it is the empty sum), so the hypothesis is false for \gamma = 0. Since we assume the hypothesis holds, we must have \gamma \neq 0.

*Step B: \mathrm{lev}(Z) = d for every representative.* Let Z = \sum_i n_i Z_i be any d-cycle representative of \gamma. Since \gamma \neq 0, we have Z \neq 0 (if Z = 0 then \gamma = [0] = 0, contradicting Step A). By the hypothesis, there exists an index j such that \dim p_1(Z_j) = \dim p_2(Z_j) = d. Then
  \dim p_1(Z_j) + \dim p_2(Z_j) - d = d + d - d = d.
Therefore
  \mathrm{lev}(Z) = \max_i (\dim p_1(Z_i) + \dim p_2(Z_i) - d) \geq \dim p_1(Z_j) + \dim p_2(Z_j) - d = d.
By the corollary (Z \neq 0), \mathrm{lev}(Z) \leq d. Hence \mathrm{lev}(Z) = d.

*Step C: \ell(\gamma) = d.* Since \mathrm{lev}(Z) = d for every d-cycle representative Z of \gamma, the minimum over all representatives is d:
  \ell(\gamma) = \min \{\mathrm{lev}(Z') : Z' \text{ represents } \gamma\} = d. \square

This completes the proof of the biconditional.
